issues.legal_issue: A court retains discretion to relieve a tenant from striking off the defence for failure to comply with a rent-deposit direction in an eviction suit.
material_facts: The landlord brought an eviction suit on the ground of non-payment of rent, and the tenant contested the claim.
The court directed the tenant to deposit arrears and continue depositing rent during the suit.
The tenant did not comply with the deposit direction without irregularity, and the landlord sought to have the defence struck off.
The governing rent-control law was enacted to protect tenants from unreasonable eviction.
issues.conclusion: The word ‘shall’ does not make striking off the defence an inevitable consequence of every failure to comply. The court retains discretion to grant relief where the circumstances and the ends of justice warrant it.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 11A of the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947, the power to direct deposits is accompanied by a sanction for non-compliance, but the direction to strike off the defence is directory, not mandatory. Whether ‘shall’ is mandatory depends on legislative intent, the nature and purpose of the law, and the consequences of the competing constructions. The Court relied on Govindlal Chagganlal Patel v. Agricultural Produce Market Committee, which approved the approach in Crawford on Statutory Construction, and on Shyamcharan Sharma v. Dharamdas, which recognized a court’s jurisdiction to extend time for rent deposits under a similar provision. Section 148 of the Code of Civil Procedure also supports the principle that a court may enlarge a period it has fixed.

rule.if: tenant_eviction_suit and rent_deposit_direction and tenant_failed_to_comply and rent_law_aims_to_prevent_unreasonable_eviction

predicates.tenant_eviction_suit: A landlord brought a suit seeking eviction of a tenant.
predicates.rent_deposit_direction: The court directed the tenant to deposit rent during the eviction suit.
predicates.tenant_failed_to_comply: The tenant failed to comply with the court’s rent-deposit direction.
predicates.rent_law_aims_to_prevent_unreasonable_ev: The governing rent law is intended to protect tenants from unreasonable eviction.

issues.definition: When a tenant fails to comply with a rent-deposit direction in an eviction suit governed by a law intended to prevent unreasonable eviction, the court may relieve the tenant from having the defence struck off.

issues.legal_issue: An irregularity in rent deposits does not require the tenant’s defence to be struck off when the tenant has deposited all arrears and the irregularity does not warrant that consequence.
material_facts: The tenant’s defence in the eviction suit was at risk of being struck off for irregularities in rent deposits.
The tenant had deposited all rent arrears.
The Supreme Court found that the irregularity was not of a nature warranting the striking off of the defence.
issues.conclusion: The tenant’s defence should not be struck off; the High Court’s direction to treat it as struck off was set aside, and the trial court’s order refusing to strike it off was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Section 11A of the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947, does not require the defence to be struck off for every deposit default. The court retains discretion to relieve against that consequence, including where all arrears have been paid and the irregularity is not sufficiently serious. The Court applied its interpretation of ‘shall’ as directory and relied on the principles in Govindlal Chagganlal Patel v. Agricultural Produce Market Committee and Shyamcharan Sharma v. Dharamdas, as well as the discretion recognized by Section 148 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

predicates.tenant_eviction_suit: A landlord brought a suit seeking eviction of a tenant.
predicates.tenant_deposited_all_arrears: The tenant deposited all rent arrears relevant to the dispute.
predicates.deposit_irregularity_not_serious: The court found that the irregularity in depositing rent was not serious enough to warrant striking off the defence.

issues.definition: If a tenant in an eviction suit has deposited all arrears and the court finds the deposit irregularity insufficiently serious, the tenant’s defence is not struck off.

issues.legal_issue: A rent-deposit direction made before an ex parte eviction decree remains effective when the decree is set aside and the suit is restored.
material_facts: The court had directed the tenant to deposit rent before the eviction suit was decreed ex parte.
The ex parte decree was later set aside on the tenant’s application, and the suit was restored for further proceedings.
The trial court considered the earlier deposit direction ineffective after restoration, but the Supreme Court held that view unsustainable.
issues.conclusion: The earlier deposit direction remained effective after the ex parte decree was set aside and the suit was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Section 11A of the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947, permits directions for deposit of arrears and continuing rent during an eviction suit. Setting aside an ex parte decree and restoring the suit does not render the earlier deposit direction ineffective. The Court disapproved the trial court’s contrary view while holding that the separate consequence of striking off the defence remained discretionary.

rule.if: tenant_eviction_suit and rent_deposit_direction_made_before_ex_parte_decree and ex_parte_decree_set_aside and suit_restored

predicates.tenant_eviction_suit: A landlord brought a suit seeking eviction of a tenant.
predicates.rent_deposit_direction_made_before_ex_pa: The court directed the tenant to deposit rent before entering an ex parte decree in the eviction suit.
predicates.ex_parte_decree_set_aside: The court set aside the ex parte decree.
predicates.suit_restored: The eviction suit was restored for further proceedings.

issues.definition: When an eviction suit is restored after its ex parte decree is set aside, a rent-deposit direction made earlier in that suit remains effective.
